idiom_name: protected virtual seam + test subclass with override
implementation_notes: The canonical C++ form: keep the dependency call in a protected virtual member function and let a test-only subclass override it; the seam must be virtual, because a non-virtual member is bound statically and the override would never run - the single most common failure of the pattern in C++. The base class needs a virtual destructor before it is used polymorphically, visibility typically has to be relaxed from private to protected (Meszaros's visibility note), and the subclass usually adds a setter that becomes the test's control point. Prefer injecting a Clock& or std::function where the class can still be changed; this variant is the fallback for third-party or frozen headers.
pitfalls: Overriding a non-virtual member compiles and silently keeps calling the base implementation; always write `override` so the compiler checks the seam.
A private virtual function can only be overridden if the subclass is a nested/friend type - in practice the seam must be protected.
Subclassing a class with a non-virtual destructor and deleting through a base pointer is undefined behaviour; and passing the subclass by value slices it back to the base type.

variants.name: GoogleMock mock class (MOCK_METHOD overrides)
variants.implementation_notes: GoogleMock automates the behaviour, not the structure: the test still declares a subclass of the class under test and writes MOCK_METHOD for the boundary, and gmock supplies expectation matching, actions and call recording on top of it. The method must be virtual, so gmock cannot open a non-virtual seam, and the mock method is declared in the public section even when the base declares it protected. Choose this variant when the test needs argument matchers, call counts or a mock reused across tests; the hand-written override stays simpler for a single canned value.
pitfalls: MOCK_METHOD must sit in a public section even if the base declares the seam protected, otherwise ON_CALL/EXPECT_CALL cannot reference it.
NiceMock/StrictMock only modulate the methods declared in the mock class itself; inherited base methods are not covered.
A mock with no EXPECT_CALL still counts as an unused mock under --gmock_verbose warnings, and gmock's C++14 baseline must be met by the toolchain.
